paper_information.title: Diseases and Disorders of Cotton: A Field Guide for symptom-based identification and management
paper_information.journal_or_source: ICAR-AICRP on Cotton, ICAR-CICR Regional Station, Coimbatore
paper_information.abstract_summary: A comprehensive field guide for symptom-based identification and management of various cotton diseases, disorders, and nutritional deficiencies in India, detailing causal agents, symptoms, epidemiology, and integrated disease management practices.
paper_information.research_objective: To help agricultural scientists, extension personnel, students, and cotton farmers identify common diseases, disorders, and biosecurity threats of cotton in India and provide location-specific management practices.
important_findings: Shift in disease prevalence over the last two decades due to climate change and adoption of Bt-cotton hybrids.
Emergence and increasing threats of target leaf spots, TSV, boll rots, bacterial leaf blight, alternaria leaf spot, and grey mildew.
Comprehensive detailing of symptom progression, disease development, and economic losses for major cotton diseases.

diseases.causal_agent: Cotton-infecting begomoviruses (family Geminiviridae) with alpha and beta satellites

general: Thickening and darkening of veins seen against sunlight (SVT type)
Upward or downward curling of leaves
Secondary leaf-like structures originating from nectaries (enations)
Stunted growth and dwarf appearance with reduced internodal length
early_symptoms: Small and large vein thickening and darkening on the underside of new leaves
advanced_symptoms: Severe leaf curling, enations on leaves and bracts, extreme stunting
visual_field_symptoms: Stunted plants showing bushy and dwarf appearance with curled leaves on top of the plant and branches

field_identification: Observe new leaves on top of plant for vein thickening and upward/downward curling

causes_and_risk_factors: Spread by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
Presence of weed, ornamental, and vegetable alternate hosts (~26 genera)

other_conditions: Presence of vector Bemisia tabaci and alternate hosts

disease_development_and_spread: Spread by whitefly Bemisia tabaci vector; symptoms can appear at seedling stage (~30 DAS) onwards
epidemiology: PDI increases slowly during June and reaches up to 80% during August and September in the north zone.
severity_and_yield_loss: Average yield loss corresponding to disease rating scales 1 to 6 recorded to be 15, 28, 38.6, 49.1, 59.1, and 72.1% in Bt cotton hybrids.

cultural_management: Cultivation of Desi cotton/sorghum/pearl millet/maize as border rows
Avoid growing whitefly and CLCuD host crops near cotton

chemical_management.timing: At fortnightly interval starting from 30 days after sowing (3-5 sprays)

chemical_management.active_ingredient_or_product: Butter milk / Cow urine + Calcium nitrate + mustard oil
chemical_management.dose: 5% / cow urine + Calcium nitrate (6.6%+0.5%) or mustard oil (3.0%)

integrated_management: Grow recommended Bt hybrids/varieties resistant/tolerant to CLCuD
Vector management using appropriate insecticides for adults and nymphs

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: Recommended Bt hybrids/varieties resistant/tolerant to CLCuD
prevention: Destroy volunteer/ratoon/infected cotton plants and weed hosts
farmer_action_points: Monitor whitefly populations and remove alternate hosts
research_findings: Incidence is increasing in Bt and non-Bt hybrids in the north zone.

diseases.causal_agent: Tobacco streak virus (genus Ilarvirus, family Bromoviridae)

general: Chlorosis of young leaves at tip, discoloration, bronzing, necrosis
Veinal chlorosis, curling of leaves, necrotic streaks on petioles, stem, and flowers
Dwarfing or stunting of plants, square drying and dropping
early_symptoms: Acute or necrotic stage: local lesions appear as rings, solid necrotic spots, or diamond-shaped patterns
advanced_symptoms: Chronic stage: leaves thicker than normal with smoother texture, tubular corolla splits with separated bracts
visual_field_symptoms: Necrotic symptoms starting from top to bottom, square drying on plants

field_identification: Observe newer leaves and tips for chlorosis, necrosis, and square drying
differential_diagnosis: Resembles physiological or nutritional disorders and herbicide phytotoxicity

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted through pollen assisted by thrips (Thripidae)
Abundance of infected pollen of parthenium, thrips population and movement

favorable_conditions.temperature: Above 30°C causes severe symptoms like large necrotic arcs, broken rings, lines, and dots
other_conditions: Presence of parthenium weed hosts and thrips vectors

disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted via thrips-assisted pollen transfer; asymptomatic infection in weed hosts like parthenium
severity_and_yield_loss: Infection at early or mid-growth stage results in severe reduction in yield and premature plant death. 12.6 to 38.8% occurrence in Tamil Nadu (2010).
farmer_action_points: Manage thrips and remove parthenium weeds
research_findings: Emerging disease in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Maharashtra.

diseases.causal_agent: Cotton Leaf Roll Dwarf Virus (genus Polerovirus, family Luteoviridae)

general: Stunting, leaf rolling, intense green foliage, vein yellowing, brittleness of leaves
Reduced flower and boll size, sometimes resulting in plant sterility
visual_field_symptoms: Stunted plants with intense green, rolled leaves starting from top to bottom

field_identification: Check for intense green foliage, leaf rolling, and stunting on newer leaves

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted by aphid (Aphis gossypii) in a circulative-persistent manner
disease_development_and_spread: Spread by Aphis gossypii
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses of up to 80% from susceptible cultivars reported in South America.
farmer_action_points: Monitor and control aphid populations
research_findings: Only one report from Maharashtra in India (2011).

diseases.causal_agent: Cotton Leaf Crumple Virus (bipartite DNA begomovirus)

general: Leaf crumpling, downward curling
Interveinal hypertrophy, foliar mosaic, puckering
Shortening of internodes, stunting
visual_field_symptoms: Stunted plants with crumpled, puckered, and downward-curled leaves

field_identification: Observe leaves for crumpling, puckering, and downward curling without vein thickening
differential_diagnosis: Similar to CLCuD except for small vein darkening and vein thickening

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted by whitefly Bemisia tabaci
Ratooning (pruning and allowing cotton to regrow)
disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted by whitefly
severity_and_yield_loss: Severe outbreaks may be exacerbated by ratooning.
farmer_action_points: Control whitefly, avoid ratooning
research_findings: Occurs in southwestern USA and Mexico; one early report in Maharashtra, India without further confirmation.

diseases.causal_agent: Cotton virescence-associated phytoplasmas ('Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris', group 16SrI)

general: Cessation of internode elongation, reduction in leaf size, stunting
Conversion of entire inflorescence into phyllody or malformation
Twisted, rolled leaves with abnormal color, closely arranged on top of stem
Witches' broom symptoms, hairy roots
advanced_symptoms: Dwarfing, resetting, or elongation with early senescence
visual_field_symptoms: Plants showing yellowing, reddening, stunting, and floral malformation

field_identification: Look for floral malformation into leaves, little leaf symptoms, and witches' broom

causes_and_risk_factors: Transmitted by brown leafhopper/jassids Orosius cellulosus
Presence of Sida spp. and Mitracarpus scaber reservoirs

other_conditions: Presence of leafhopper vectors and Sida weed reservoirs

disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted by leafhopper vectors
epidemiology: In Mali, up to 50% of plants infected in some fields.
farmer_action_points: Monitor host plants and insect vectors
research_findings: Recorded in Western Africa; little leaf symptoms observed in New Delhi (2010) with homology to 16SrI group.

diseases.causal_agent: Rhizoctonia bataticola = Macrophomina phaseolina, Rhizoctonia solani, Sclerotium delphinii, Sclerotium rolfsii

general: Wilting of plant foliage from top to bottom
Leaves remain attached to branches/stem
Dry or wet dark rot of lower stem followed by shredding of bark
Discolored stele and pith, black dot-like sclerotia beneath bark
early_symptoms: Yellow patch on lower stem which later turns black, drying of seedlings
advanced_symptoms: Dissolution of stem and root tissues, minute sclerotia
visual_field_symptoms: Plants wilting in circular patches in the field that expand year after year

field_identification: Check for circular patches of wilted plants, bark shredding at base, and easy pulling from ground

causes_and_risk_factors: Soil-borne fungi surviving in soil and crop debris

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Prevalent in sandy soils, alluvial soils, and heavy clays (black cotton soils)

disease_development_and_spread: Occurs in circular patches; M. phaseolina at seedling stage (60 DAS) or after wood formation; R. solani at 30 DAS and severe at 90-120 DAS
severity_and_yield_loss: Serious in northern India, affects both G. hirsutum and G. arboreum, being more serious in desi cotton.

biological_management: Seed treatment with Trichoderma harzianum @ 4 g/kg or T. viride @ 4 g/kg or Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/kg
Soil application of Trichoderma spp. and/or P. fluorescens @ 2.5 kg/ha in 250 kg vermicompost/FYM
integrated_management: Seed treatment combined with soil application of bioagents and spot drenching of Carbendazim

prevention: Avoid planting seeds from infested regions
farmer_action_points: Spot-treat affected patches with Carbendazim or bioagents

diseases.causal_agent: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum (Atk.)

general: Wilting of plant foliage from top to bottom
Darkening of veins on cotyledons, peripheral chlorosis and necrosis
Yellowing at margin of lower leaves, chlorosis in patches between main veins
early_symptoms: Darkening of veins on cotyledons at seedling stage
advanced_symptoms: Shedding of all leaves before stem dries out
visual_field_symptoms: Wilting and drying of plants in patches in the field

field_identification: Check for wilting in patches and make a cross-section of stem near root zone to observe xylem color change

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed and soil-borne fungal pathogen surviving on seed and crop residues via chlamydospores
disease_development_and_spread: Appears generally between 30 to 120 DAS; colonizes roots and grows systemically into vascular tissues
severity_and_yield_loss: Loss may vary from field to field and variety to variety from 5 to 40%.

integrated_management: Grow resistant diploid varieties (upland cotton/Bt hybrids are immune to Indian race 4 of this pathogen)

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: Upland cotton / Bt hybrids are immune to the Indian race of the pathogen
farmer_action_points: Grow resistant upland Bt hybrids where diploid wilt is a problem
warnings_and_limitations: Occurs only in diploid cotton in India
research_findings: Fusarium wilt has become less important as upland cotton is grown in >90% area and is immune to the Indian race.

diseases.causal_agent: Verticillium dahliae Kleb.

general: Drooping branches and leaves
Interveinal chlorosis followed by yellowing, leaf scorching
Drying of leaf margins and areas between veins ("Tiger stripe symptoms")
Defoliation, plant death, flecked brown or pink discoloration of vascular tissues
advanced_symptoms: Death of entire plant, smaller bolls, pinkish discoloration in stem and wood
visual_field_symptoms: Wilted plants showing tiger stripe leaf symptoms and vascular discoloration

field_identification: Check for tiger stripe leaf symptoms and cut stem cross/diagonally at base to observe brown/pink vascular discoloration
diagnostic_methods: Cutting stem at base to check vascular discoloration
differential_diagnosis: Can be easily mistaken for Fusarium wilt

causes_and_risk_factors: Soil-borne pathogen infecting through roots
Extended wet or overcast weather, waterlogging, late-maturing crops, cooler weather
disease_development_and_spread: Infects plants at seedling stage and grows continuously with plant; first symptoms appear 90-100 DAS at squaring/boll formation
severity_and_yield_loss: Plants may remain barren during severe weather conditions.

biological_management: Seed treatment with T. viride @ 10g/kg or P. fluorescens @ 10g/kg
Soil application of T. viride or P. fluorescens @ 1 kg/acre with 100 kg FYM or vermicompost

chemical_management.application_method: Seed treatment and soil drenching at base of infected plants
Soil drenching at base of infected plants

integrated_management: Seed treatment, soil application of bioagents, balanced nutrition, and soil drenching

susceptible_varieties: G. hirsutum, G. barbadense, G. herbaceum, G. arboreum
farmer_action_points: Avoid waterlogging and late irrigation that exposes crop to cooler weather
warnings_and_limitations: Restricted mainly to south zone in India

diseases.causal_agent: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum race-4 (FOV4)

general: Seedling damping-off, leaf wilt, chlorosis, vascular discoloration
Black streaking at the center of root limited to roots at initial flowering stage
Root decay, wilting, and death
early_symptoms: Earliest wilting symptoms on seedlings in cotyledons
advanced_symptoms: Severe plant stunting (>80%), seedling death, bare spots in field
visual_field_symptoms: Random bare spots in fields where seedlings are killed, increasing in size over years

field_identification: Look for random bare spots in fields, seedling damping-off, and black streaking in root center
diagnostic_methods: Quarantine evaluation of imported seed and soil material
differential_diagnosis: Resembles disease caused by other fungal pathogens like FOV and Rhizoctonia solani

causes_and_risk_factors: Soil-borne and seed-borne fungus
Movement of infested seeds or soil due to tillage or furrow irrigation, farm implements
disease_development_and_spread: Fungus produces spores persisting in soil and crop residue; spread by water, implements, and contaminated acid-delinted seeds
severity_and_yield_loss: Ability to kill seedlings and cause severe stunting greater than 80%.
prevention: Do not save and replant seed from infested fields
Clean farm equipment with pressure washer and detergent
farmer_action_points: Keep constant watch on movement of cotton seeds and material
warnings_and_limitations: Biosecurity threat; extremely virulent and causes severe early-season damage in absence of nematodes
research_findings: Race 4 detected in USA (California, Texas, New Mexico, Kansas); first described in India in 1960 on G. arboreum.

diseases.causal_agent: Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum (Smith) Vauterin et al. (Xcm)

general: Water-soaked, angular leaf spots restricted by veins
Dark brown necrotic spots, 'shot-hole' appearance when necrotic tissue falls away
Vein blight (main veins as black streaks)
Black arm (elongated grayish-to-black lesions on stem)
Boll rot phase (small round water-soaked spots turning sunken and brown)
early_symptoms: Tiny round to elongate lesions on cotyledons, deep green and water-soaked spots
advanced_symptoms: Defoliation, stem cankers girdling and killing seedlings, extensive boll rotting
visual_field_symptoms: Angular dark brown spots on leaves, black streaks on veins, and black lesions on stems and bolls

field_identification: Observe underside of leaves for water-soaking around angular dark brown lesions

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed and plant debrisborne bacterium; favored by wet weather
disease_development_and_spread: Occurs from seedling to boll development stages (45 to 105 DAS); four phases: seedling phase, angular leaf spot, vein blight, black arm, and boll rot
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield loss up to 20%; potential yield loss estimated to be 22% with max disease index of 28.8% at Dharwad, Guntur, Surat, and Akola.

biological_management: Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10g/kg or Trichoderma

chemical_management.number_of_applications: 3-4 times at fortnightly intervals starting 50 DAS

integrated_management: Seed treatment with fungicides/bioagents and foliar sprays of copper oxychloride

susceptible_varieties: Bt hybrids have manifested more susceptibility to bacterial blight compared to non-Bt counterparts
farmer_action_points: Apply copper oxychloride sprays upon initial appearance of water-soaked spots
warnings_and_limitations: Resurgence observed in central and south India in Bt hybrids

diseases.causal_agent: Exact cause uncertain; unique strain of Agrobacterium tumefaciens reported in Texas on taproot brown scars

general: Bronze or red discoloration and wilting of leaves ("bronzing")
Rapid wilting, collapse of youngest leaves in terminal, increase in leaf temperature
Reddening of stem and fruit shed
early_symptoms: Mild bronze leaf tint, lower leaf angle (wilting), higher leaf temperature in upper canopy
advanced_symptoms: Necrosis of stem tissue or whole plants, fruit shed, plant death
visual_field_symptoms: Sporadic occurrence of plants across field showing copper top / bronze red discoloration and wilting

field_identification: Check for sporadic bronze/red discoloration, rapid wilting, and brown scars on taproots
differential_diagnosis: Resembles Fusarium and Verticillium wilts, Macrophomina root rots, nematode damage, nutrient deficiencies, and drought

causes_and_risk_factors: Daytime temperatures above 32°C for 2-3 weeks
High light intensity, high nitrogen fertilizer rates, phosphorus/sulfur/potassium deficiencies, high soil pH (>7), drought followed by rain/irrigation

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Drought followed by rain or irrigation
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: High soil pH (above 7), nutrient deficiencies (P, S, K)

disease_development_and_spread: Occurs especially during boll development stage, often appearing first at row ends or field margins
severity_and_yield_loss: Devastating losses occurred in 1998 in USA (e.g., Georgia losses valued at nearly $25 million).
susceptible_varieties: Short-season varieties of Upland and Pima cotton
farmer_action_points: Manage irrigation and nitrogen fertilization to avoid stress conditions
warnings_and_limitations: Biosecurity threat; mysterious disease with uncertain exact cause
research_findings: Reported in Midsouth and Southeast USA during hot summers of 1995, 1996, and 1998.

diseases.causal_agent: Alternaria spp. including Alternaria macrospora Zimm., Alternaria alternata (Fr.) Keissler

general: Small dull and dark brown, circular or irregularly shaped spots with concentric rings
Spots with purple margins on senescing leaves
Lesions becoming gray and dry with 'shot-holed' appearance
Coalescing spots forming large burnt/blighted patches leading to defoliation
early_symptoms: Spots on cotyledons causing them to shed
advanced_symptoms: Severe defoliation, burnt/blighted leaves
visual_field_symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings starting from lower to upper leaves across canopy, associated with reddening and yellowing

field_identification: Check for dark brown to black spots with concentric rings from lower to upper leaves, wider than target leaf spots
differential_diagnosis: Similar to Stemphylium leaf spot and Target leaf spot

causes_and_risk_factors: Insufficient potassium availability either due to inadequate fertilization or drought
Late-season cotton development
disease_development_and_spread: Appears at boll formation stages; natural infection of seeds or seed inoculation results in cotyledon infection
epidemiology: Erratic in occurrence, causing severe defoliation in some years.
severity_and_yield_loss: Potential yield loss estimated to be 26.6% with maximum disease index 31.6% at Rahuri, Guntur, and Dharwad (Monga et al. 2013).

integrated_management: Balanced fertilization (potassium) combined with timely fungicide sprays

susceptible_varieties: G. hirsutum, G. barbadense, interspecific hybrids, Bt hybrids
farmer_action_points: Monitor potassium levels and apply recommended fungicides during boll development
warnings_and_limitations: Bt hybrids have manifested more susceptibility to Alternaria leaf spots
research_findings: Showing increasing trend in South and Central India.

diseases.causal_agent: Cercospora gossypina Cke. (perfect state: Mycosphaerella gossypina (Cke.) Atk.)

general: Reddish spots on cotyledons and early crop stages
Lesions enlarging with white to light brown center and distinct dark brown/blackish rim
Concentric zones with red color at margins, enlarging up to 10 mm
Grey center that cracks and drops down giving target board appearance in advanced stage
early_symptoms: Reddish spots on cotyledons and early leaves
advanced_symptoms: Withering of large leaf patches, ragged margins, pale withered leaves dropping
visual_field_symptoms: Concentric spots with grey cracking centers and dark margins on older leaves

field_identification: Check for circular spots with grey cracking centers and dark margins; microscopic examination of whip-like septate spores needed for exact diagnosis
diagnostic_methods: Viewing long, thin whip-like, septate spores
differential_diagnosis: Difficult to differentiate from Alternaria, Corynespora, and Myrothecium leaf spots in the field

causes_and_risk_factors: Favorable weather under wet soil conditions when plants are unthrifty
disease_development_and_spread: Usually affects older leaves, spreading over whole plant in favorable wet weather
severity_and_yield_loss: Considered a minor disease and not considered to be a cause of yield loss.
research_findings: Occurs only sporadically in India and is not a serious hazard.

diseases.causal_agent: Corynespora cassiicola (Berk. & Curt.) Wei.

general: Small brown to brick-red circular to irregular spots leading to large spots (~1 inch / 2 cm)
Series of concentric rings with necrotic tissue and depression at center ("target spot" symptoms)
Dark red spots 2 mm to 10 mm in size, primarily in lower canopy
early_symptoms: Small brown to brick-red circular spots appearing as early as 60-70 DAS
advanced_symptoms: Coalescing lesions, severe necrosis, premature senescence and dropping of leaves (premature defoliation)
visual_field_symptoms: Interior canopy defoliation starting from bottom and progressing upwards, with target-pattern spots on leaves and bracts

field_identification: Check for interior canopy leaf spots with concentric rings and depression, not bordered by dark band, starting at bottom
differential_diagnosis: Differentiated from Stemphylium/Alternaria by location in canopy and absence of dark border band

causes_and_risk_factors: Frequent showers/irrigation, dense crop canopy creating microclimate, high humidity
disease_development_and_spread: Spores spread through wind and rain splash; soil and partially seed-borne, overwintering in plant debris
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses 5-40% when disease occurs early in season (at bloom) causing 10-50% defoliation.
susceptible_varieties: Various cotton cultivars and Bt hybrids depending on susceptibility
farmer_action_points: Monitor lower canopy during humid weather for early target spot lesions
warnings_and_limitations: Emerging disease with increasing trend in central and southern zones
research_findings: Reported across multiple regions in India (North Maharashtra, Nagpur, Guntur).

diseases.causal_agent: Myrothecium roridum Tode

general: Light brown to light ash color small circular to oval spots (2-10 mm) with dark brown/violet to reddish-brown margin
Conspicuous rings of pinhead size black sporodochia in concentric rings on spots (upper and lower leaf surface)
Shot-hole appearance where center drops out, heavy defoliation
early_symptoms: Small circular to oval light brown spots with dark margins
advanced_symptoms: Coalescing spots forming large patches, leaf shedding, boll lesions damaging lint making it brittle and discolored (strained yellow/light brown)
visual_field_symptoms: Spots with concentric black fungal fruiting bodies (sporodochia) on leaves and bolls

field_identification: Check for light ash spots with dark margins and concentric rings of black sporodochia

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed-borne pathogen; favored by prolonged rainfall and humidity
disease_development_and_spread: Seed-borne; occurs all over India, severe in wet conditions
severity_and_yield_loss: Potential yield loss estimated to be 29.2% with maximum disease index 22.5% at Khandwa (Monga et al. 2013); losses estimated at 15% with 37% disease intensity.
susceptible_varieties: G. hirsutum and G. barbadense are more severely attacked than other species
farmer_action_points: Inspect seeds and plants during prolonged wet periods
warnings_and_limitations: Prevalent and severe in Madhya Pradesh (Khandwa)

diseases.causal_agent: Colletotrichum gossypii Southw. (perfect stage: Glomerella gossypii), Colletotrichum capsici (Syd.) Butl. & Bisby

general: Reddish brown or dark brown lesions just below ground level on seedlings
Small circular sunken reddish to brown spots on leaf margins or near tips (5-10 mm)
Stem canker spots (small reddish/brown with depression in center turning black)
Reddish-brown to purplish-brown spots on bolls with depressed center, turning black with reddish margin
early_symptoms: Spots on cotyledons with irregular necrotic margins; lesions on hypocotyl causing seedling collapse
advanced_symptoms: Defoliation, salmon-pink conidial masses on spots in moist weather, internal boll lint discoloration (compact, discolored pinkish-brown)
visual_field_symptoms: Sunken reddish-brown leaf spots, stem cankers, and bolls with pink spore masses

field_identification: Check for sunken reddish-brown leaf spots near margins, stem cankers, and salmon-pink spore masses on bolls

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed infestation; favored by humid microclimate and irrigation
disease_development_and_spread: Affects plant from 20 DAS to boll maturation; seed-borne origin
severity_and_yield_loss: Losses have decreased to negligible proportions; occasionally noticed in southern and central parts of India.
farmer_action_points: Examine seedlings and bolls for sunken spots and pink spore masses

diseases.causal_agent: Helminthosporium gossypii Tucker

general: Numerous circular light brown spots on lower leaves (0.5-2.5 mm)
Spots turning ashy in center with dark purple ring around them
Tissue in center drops down leaving holes ('shot-holes')
early_symptoms: Circular light brown spots on lower leaves
advanced_symptoms: Early defoliation when disease is severe
visual_field_symptoms: Small spots with ashy centers and purple rings on lower leaves, causing drop-out holes

field_identification: Check lower leaves for small circular light brown spots with purple rings and ashy centers

causes_and_risk_factors: Pathogen overwinters on diseased plant debris, particularly dead leaves during off-season
disease_development_and_spread: Occurs sporadically on lower leaves
severity_and_yield_loss: Does not cause any noticeable loss in yield and is considered a minor disease.

cultural_management: Remove or destroy crop debris and dead leaves

susceptible_varieties: All four cultivated species of Gossypium including tree cotton
farmer_action_points: Clear off-season crop debris
research_findings: Observed in cotton-growing areas in India, especially Dharwad region of Karnataka.

diseases.causal_agent: Ascochyta gossypii Woron. (perfect stage: Phoma exigua)

general: White to light brown circular lesions approaching 2 mm (<0.1 in) enlarging into irregular necrotic spots
Narrow dark border on necrotic margins with target-like appearance
Elongated canker spots with reddish-purple to black or ash gray on stem
Rough circular lesions on bolls following boll rotting
early_symptoms: Lesions on cotyledons and leaves in 3-8 week old plants (seedling disease)
advanced_symptoms: Death of vital parts from stem cankers, partial defoliation
visual_field_symptoms: Light brown circular spots with dark borders, black fruiting structures, and stem cankers during continuous rainy periods

field_identification: Check for light brown circular spots with dark borders, shot holes, and small black fruiting structures on older lesions
differential_diagnosis: Can easily be confused with other fungal leaf blights at early stage

causes_and_risk_factors: Continuous rainy periods; wide host range serving as collateral host
disease_development_and_spread: Appears at seedling to vegetative stages (20-60 DAS); starts on lower leaves and progresses upwards
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield loss is rarely reported; prolonged rains may hinder plant stand.
farmer_action_points: Monitor crop during continuous rainy periods in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka

diseases.causal_agent: Ramularia areola Atk.

general: Irregular, angular, pale translucent spots (1-10 mm, usually 3-4 mm) restricted by major leaf veinlets ('areolae')
Frosty or mildew growth consisting of conidiophores on undersurface and subsequently upper surface
Yellowish-brown leaves as infection progresses, necrotic lesions resembling bacterial blight
early_symptoms: Angular pale translucent spots restricted by veinlets on lower to middle canopy leaves
advanced_symptoms: Premature defoliation in severe cases
visual_field_symptoms: Angular spots with white powdery/frosty fungal growth on underside of lower to middle leaves at maturity

field_identification: Check for angular spots restricted by veins with white powdery growth on leaf underside (no other common cotton disease has white powdery growth on leaf underside)
differential_diagnosis: Can easily be confused with bacterial leaf blight at an early stage

causes_and_risk_factors: Survives on infected dead leaves, perennial cotton, volunteer plants, and overlapping crops
disease_development_and_spread: Appears at vegetative to boll formation stages (60-120 DAS), starting from lower to middle canopy when plants reach maturity
severity_and_yield_loss: Potential yield loss estimated to be 25.6-46.6% at Dharwad, Guntur, and Nanded (Monga et al. 2013).
susceptible_varieties: Majority of released Bt hybrids fall in moderately susceptible to highly susceptible category; G. arboreum, G. herbaceum, G. hirsutum
prevention: Sanitation of infected dead leaves and volunteer plants
farmer_action_points: Inspect lower leaves for angular spots with white powdery growth and apply fungicides
warnings_and_limitations: Assumed to be serious in central and southern zones
research_findings: Showed increased incidence from 2008 to 2011 with PDI from 11.5 to 32.2%.

diseases.causal_agent: Phakospora gossypii (Arth.) Hirat. F.

general: Rusty light to brown spots on older leaves leading to premature defoliation
Uredial sori as small (1-3 mm) pinkish-brown spots coalescing into larger patches
Yellowish-brown uredia on both leaf surfaces (primary deeply immersed on upper surface, secondary shallowly seated on lower surface)
Oval to circular uredia on pedicels and branches
early_symptoms: Rusty light to brown spots on older leaves during dry season
advanced_symptoms: Heavy defoliation, decrease in photosynthetic area
visual_field_symptoms: Rusty spots with yellowish-brown uredia on older leaves during dry season (December-March)

field_identification: Check older leaves for rusty light-brown spots and yellowish-brown uredia on both leaf surfaces in dry season

causes_and_risk_factors: Favored by cooler temperatures; appears late in season after onset of senescence or in dry season (December-March)
disease_development_and_spread: Appears at flowering to boll formation stages (120-180 DAS); only uredial stage occurs in India
severity_and_yield_loss: Potential yield loss estimated to be 21.7% with max disease index of 32.8% at Dharwad; avoidable loss estimated to be 21.7% in Bunny Bt and 34.05% in RCH 2 BG II.

integrated_management: Foliar sprays of Sulphur or Propiconazole

farmer_action_points: Monitor late-sown and prolonged irrigated crops during winter months for rust pustules
warnings_and_limitations: Important problem in southern zone, causing significant yield losses when appearing early
research_findings: Severe incidence noted from 2009 to 2012 in northern Karnataka.

diseases.causal_agent: Colletotrichum gossypii var. cephalosporioides, C. gossypii, Fusarium sp., Ramularia areola, Lasiodiplodia theobromae, Myrothecium roridum, Alternaria macrospora, Phoma exigua, Phomopsis spp., Phytophthora spp., Rhizoctonia spp., C. cassiicola, Rhizopus spp., Aspergillus spp., Mucor sp., Cercospora sp., Diplodia sp., Curvularia sp., Cladosporium sp., Helminthosporium sp., Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum, etc.

general: Small brown and/or black colored dots on bolls enlarging to cover entire bolls
Growth of fungi and mycelia on infected bolls
Rotting of pericarp, seeds, and lint; premature opening of bolls or bolls never bursting and falling off prematurely
early_symptoms: Small brown or black colored dots on bolls during boll maturity and bursting stages
advanced_symptoms: Complete boll rotting, fiber quality affected, premature defoliation of bolls
visual_field_symptoms: Bolls covered with fungal mycelia and dark spots, rotting prematurely

field_identification: Check for discolored bolls with fungal growth, spots, and rotting during boll maturity stages

causes_and_risk_factors: Continuous cloudy weather, rain showers, warm weather, high relative humidity, insect-pest damage
disease_development_and_spread: Occurs during boll maturity and bursting stages (120-180 DAS); involves ~170 organisms in boll rot complex
severity_and_yield_loss: Productivity losses up to 20-30%.
farmer_action_points: Monitor bolls during humid and rainy weather for rotting spots
warnings_and_limitations: Part of complex boll rot problem impacting lint production and quality

diseases.causal_agent: Pantoea agglomerans, P. ananatis, P. dispersa, P. anthophila, Erwinia uredovora, E. aroideae, Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum, Nigrospora oryzae, Colletotrichum gossypii, etc.

general: Early disease diagnosis complicated as outer surface of boll seems healthy
Immature diseased locule attributed to 'hard lock' having rotted seeds with brown dense lint
Partially opened bolls that drop or do not open properly
Immature seeds, fibers, and lint appearing discolored (light yellow, pink-red to brown) with slimy presence, swollen and rotted seeds
early_symptoms: Minute black spots as indicators of piercing-sucking insect feeding signs on carpel layer
advanced_symptoms: Severe necrosis and rot of flowering buds, young bolls, and seeds within older bolls, headlocks formed
visual_field_symptoms: Bolls appearing healthy outside but upon cross-sectioning show discolored rotted locules, slime, and hard lock

field_identification: Cross-section or open bolls to inspect locules and seeds for internal rotting, sliminess, and discolored lint without external symptoms

causes_and_risk_factors: Invasion of developing ovary via wounds associated with insect feeding (stink bugs, hoppers, bugs) and drizzling rains during first 3 weeks of boll development

other_conditions: Piercing-sucking bug/insect infestation during bud and boll development

disease_development_and_spread: Invades via insect-feeding wounds in first 3 weeks of boll development; opportunistic bacteria (Enterobacteriaceae) and endophytic fungi
severity_and_yield_loss: Causes 10-15% yield loss in USA and 20% in China; overall boll rot causes 20-30% loss.

integrated_management: Monitor insect populations during bud and boll development

prevention: Control sucking pests during the first 3 weeks of boll development
farmer_action_points: Cut open green bolls to check for internal slimy rot and hard locks
warnings_and_limitations: Emerging disease in central and south cotton-growing zones; difficult to diagnose without opening bolls
research_findings: Erwinia aroideae and Pantoea ananatis associated with cotton boll rot.

diseases.causal_agent: Abiotic environmental factors (waterlogging, soil saturation, high temperature, bright sunshine, poor root growth)

general: Plant starts wilting from top once water stagnation takes place in root zone
Within a few days all leaves drop off while bolls remain attached
Bolls may forcefully open just prior to harvest but will not ripen fully (poor quantity and unmarketable quality)
Spreads like wildfire covering whole field within a few hours
early_symptoms: Leaves start wilting from top to bottom within a few hours
advanced_symptoms: Leaf drop, unripened open bolls
visual_field_symptoms: Large-scale rapid wilting of canopy with leaves dropping off and bolls remaining attached, roots and stem appearing healthy inside

field_identification: Check root and stem by cross-opening (appearing healthy without fungal growth) combined with rapid top-down wilting after waterlogging/rain
diagnostic_methods: Cross-opening roots and stem to check for absence of fungi

causes_and_risk_factors: Soil saturation / water logging
Rapid growth rate at grand growth stage (high transpiration and photosynthesis)
Bright sunshine and hot air temperature (high O2 requirement in roots with limited O2 in waterlogged soil)
Clayey soils, soil hard pan/compactness, low organic carbon, early irrigation, heavy boll load

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Sudden rain followed by water stagnation, heavy irrigation
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Clayey soils, poorly drained sandy soils, soil hard pan/compactness, low organic carbon

disease_development_and_spread: Occurs from flowering onwards; lack of oxygen leads to death of roots and root hairs, breaking soil-plant-atmosphere continuum
severity_and_yield_loss: Causes havoc and large-scale wilting in Bt fields across Central, South, and North zones, prominent in early maturing high-yielding Bt hybrids.

cultural_management: Avoid water stagnation and drought stress

chemical_management.timing: Immediately after appearance of wilting symptoms
Immediately after appearance of wilting symptoms
Immediately after appearance of wilting symptoms on affected plants

integrated_management: Avoid water stagnation, foliar spray of Cobalt chloride or sodium benzoate, and drenching of copper oxychloride + urea

susceptible_varieties: Early maturing and high-yielding Bt hybrids
prevention: Ensure proper field drainage to prevent waterlogging
farmer_action_points: Act within 24-48 hours of wilting symptom onset with recommended sprays and drenching
warnings_and_limitations: Can destroy whole field within a few hours

diseases.disease_name: Red Leaf or Leaf Reddening Complex
diseases.causal_agent: Abiotic stresses (nitrogen deficiency, water stagnation, high soil moisture, magnesium deficiency, cloudy weather, low night temperature, drought followed by rain/irrigation)

general: Initial symptoms appear on fully expanded leaves where area between veins in upper part becomes raised
Leaf margin becomes yellow and turns into red pigmentation covering whole leaf
Reddening progresses to other leaves and stem
Shedding of leaf and bolls due to poor plant growth
early_symptoms: Raised area between veins on fully expanded leaves, margin yellowing
advanced_symptoms: Whole leaf red pigmentation, leaf and boll shedding
visual_field_symptoms: Plants with red pigmented leaves during boll development and maturity stages

field_identification: Observe above-ground plant parts for leaf margin yellowing turning into red pigmentation during boll development

causes_and_risk_factors: Nitrogen deficiency, water stagnation, high soil moisture, magnesium deficiency, cloudy weather, low night temperature
Drought followed by rain/irrigation, high wind velocity, high solar radiation, soil with poor capacity to supply nitrogen and phosphorus

favorable_conditions.temperature: Low night temperature, high solar radiation
favorable_conditions.rainfall: Water stagnation, high soil moisture, drought followed by rain/irrigation
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Soil with poor capacity to supply nitrogen and phosphorus

disease_development_and_spread: Appears during boll development and becomes severe at boll maturity
severity_and_yield_loss: Emerged as a serious problem in various cotton-growing regions of Indian subcontinents.

cultural_management: Manage soil moisture and avoid water stagnation

chemical_management.active_ingredient_or_product: Magnesium sulphate (MgSO4) + Urea + Zinc Sulphate + Boron
chemical_management.timing: 90 days old crop, twice at 15 day intervals, followed by 2% DAP

integrated_management: Foliar nutrition sprays of MgSO4, urea, zinc sulfate, boron, and DAP

farmer_action_points: Apply recommended nutrient foliar sprays at 90 days crop stage
